fields.description_1: Course Dates Manager had to make structured course publishing easier than maintaining dates and programme information in scattered pages. The plugin uses a dedicated WordPress course content model, taxonomy, settings, a responsive shortcode and a public REST API. The challenge was to keep editing simple for administrators while exposing only the published information required by the frontend or external consumers. Queries needed sensible limits, assets had to stay scoped and uninstall behaviour had to remain controlled. The public interface also needed accessible accordion behaviour and clear course discovery on smaller screens. The portfolio text needed to show the actual WordPress engineering work rather than describe the project as a generic course website. Technical boundaries and maintainability therefore mattered as much as the visible course overview.
fields.description_2: I built Course Dates Manager around a dedicated course post type and taxonomy, giving administrators one structured place to maintain programme information. A responsive shortcode renders the public overview, while paginated REST endpoints expose only published course data for controlled integrations. The frontend uses lightweight JavaScript and accessible accordion behaviour instead of a heavy framework. Settings are sanitized, assets load only where needed and queries are bounded so the plugin remains predictable as content grows. Lifecycle and uninstall handling are conservative. The result connects editorial management with a reusable public presentation without unnecessary dependencies. The portfolio solution explains the content model, API boundary and frontend behaviour directly, based on repository evidence rather than unsupported claims about student engagement, registrations or learning outcomes.

fields.description_1: AI Patch Runner had to make plugin code changes reviewable without turning a WordPress admin tool into an unrestricted production patch system. Structured JSON patches can affect installed plugin files, so a mistake could break functionality or leave no clear recovery path. The workflow needed preview, apply and rollback stages with strong permission boundaries. Production applies also had to be blocked by default and require trusted server configuration plus an explicit interface setting. Multisite adds another privilege boundary because plugin updates require super-admin control. The portfolio text needed to make those safeguards clear instead of presenting automation as automatically safe. The central problem was controlled change management: show what will happen, restrict where it can happen and preserve rollback.
fields.description_2: I built AI Patch Runner as an admin-only WordPress plugin for reviewing, previewing, applying and rolling back structured JSON patch packages. Preview remains separate from execution so a change can be inspected before plugin files are modified. Production application is disabled by default and only becomes available when a trusted server-side constant and the matching admin setting both allow it. Plugin-update capabilities gate normal use, while multisite requires super-admin access. Rollback is part of the same workflow rather than an afterthought. The project focuses on controlled patch packages, not arbitrary code generation or remote execution. The portfolio solution explains the safety model and reversible process directly, without claiming automation removes the need for staging, technical review or reliable backups.

fields.description_1: ACF CSV Manager addressed a content-management problem: structured WordPress data is difficult to review when fields are spread across many editing screens. The project focused on exporting ACF-oriented content to CSV and returning reviewed updates through a controlled workflow. Bulk work creates extra risk because incorrect rows or mismatched fields can affect many items at once. The repository is now a retired duplicate of ACF Page Text Manager, so the portfolio story also needs to reflect that historical role accurately. It should not present this older repository as the current canonical product. The problem therefore combines workflow efficiency with maintenance clarity: support structured review while avoiding duplicate active codebases, repeated fixes and unclear ownership for future releases.
fields.description_2: I developed ACF CSV Manager as an earlier export and import workflow for ACF-related WordPress content. It showed how page data could move into a reviewable spreadsheet format and return through a controlled admin process instead of editing every item separately. As the project evolved, its functionality and plugin identity overlapped with ACF Page Text Manager. I therefore consolidated active development into the canonical ACF-Text-Manager repository rather than maintaining two independent copies with duplicate fixes, releases and documentation. The older repository remains available for history and rollback while migration guidance points users toward the maintained version. The portfolio solution explains both the original bulk-content problem and the later maintenance decision without presenting the retired repository as the active product source.

fields.description_1: Modern Image Manager had to bring WordPress media maintenance into one safer admin workflow. Image titles, alt text, captions, descriptions, filenames, usage information and exported files can otherwise require several separate screens or manual processes. Bulk import and rename features increase the risk because malformed CSV data, unsafe paths or extension changes can damage media references. The plugin also needed to handle large libraries without loading every attachment into memory at once. Deletion behaviour had to respect WordPress media-trash settings rather than force permanent removal. The portfolio text needed to explain the real media-management scope without implying that every cleanup action is harmless. The core problem was combining practical editing, scanning and export tools with capability checks, input validation, bounded processing and conservative file handling.
fields.description_2: I built Modern Image Manager as a WordPress admin interface for media metadata, CSV import and export, usage scanning and media ZIP exports. Update and import handlers validate request data, file types and upload paths before changes are accepted. Filename edits preserve the existing extension, and metadata is saved only after a requested rename succeeds so a failed file operation does not create a partial update. Large media scans run in batches instead of loading the whole library into memory. CSV exports guard against spreadsheet formula injection, while import, export and ZIP actions use capability and nonce checks. Attachment deletion follows normal WordPress behaviour rather than forcing permanent deletion. The solution combines practical media management with explicit safeguards around higher-risk operations that require careful review.

fields.description_1: ACF Page Text Manager had to solve fragmented WordPress content editing. Page titles, excerpts, ACF values, Yoast or Rank Math metadata and image text can live in different admin screens, which makes structured review and bulk updates slow. Importing spreadsheets introduces extra risk because files can contain unsupported fields, unsafe archives or media rename instructions that should not run automatically. The plugin therefore needed one focused editing surface plus controlled CSV and XLSX workflows without becoming a general migration tool. ACF compatibility, temporary-file cleanup and conservative uninstall behaviour also mattered. The portfolio text needed to explain both the editorial value and the safeguards around bulk writes. The main challenge was centralising supported text work while keeping scope, validation and higher-risk media operations explicit and predictable.
fields.description_2: I built ACF Page Text Manager around one WordPress admin screen for supported core fields, ACF text fields, SEO metadata and image text. Editors can update values inline, export selected items to CSV or XLSX and import reviewed files through validated preparation and processing. The plugin dynamically discovers supported ACF fields rather than assuming one fixed project layout. Uploaded files use bounded validation and temporary storage that is cleaned after processing. Physical media filename changes remain an explicit opt-in path and require additional confirmation, including a separate WP-CLI flag for command-line imports. The plugin checks ACF availability and limits uninstall cleanup to plugin-owned settings and temporary state. The result improves structured content review without treating bulk editing as an unrestricted write operation.

fields.description_1: SEO Image Assistant had to connect image research with WordPress page context instead of treating stock-image selection as a separate manual task. The plugin combines Shutterstock OAuth, keyword and page-based search, ACF image-field mapping, suggestion queues, licensed downloads and recovery tools. That creates several risk points: external credentials, licensing state, file validation and writes into structured WordPress fields. Search also needs to avoid repeatedly scanning the full media library just to determine which assets were already used. The portfolio text needed to explain the workflow without suggesting that stock imagery automatically improves SEO. The actual problem was operational: help administrators find and review suitable licensed images, map them to the correct page fields and keep downloads, permissions and recovery behaviour controlled throughout the process.
fields.description_2: I built SEO Image Assistant for Shutterstock as a WordPress workflow that starts with page or keyword context and ends with a reviewed image assignment. OAuth connects the site to Shutterstock, while search and suggestion queues help administrators evaluate assets before licensing. Supported ACF image fields can be mapped to the selected page context, and licensed downloads are validated for allowed MIME type and file-size limits before import. Successful items from partial licensing responses remain recoverable instead of being discarded with failed items. REST endpoints are capability-gated, and uninstall data removal is disabled by default. The plugin keeps a stored used-ID index instead of scanning every attachment for each search. The solution focuses on controlled image workflow and licensing boundaries, not unsupported ranking claims.

fields.description_1: Webactueel Translate had to make multilingual WordPress work manageable when source text, translated strings, SEO metadata, media, review status and import or export tasks live in different places. The plugin scans public post types, Elementor content, ACF fields and WooCommerce data, creating many contexts for the same text. AI-assisted translation adds another boundary because external providers may process submitted content and generated output still needs review. Frontend translation must avoid admin, REST, checkout and other requests where replacement could be unsafe. The portfolio text therefore needed to explain a review-first translation system rather than promise automatic quality. The challenge was combining discovery, editing, publication control, SEO support and optional AI assistance while keeping context, privacy and failure behaviour visible.
fields.description_2: I built Webactueel Translate as a WordPress workflow with language management, content scanning, visual editing, translation tables, CSV or XLIFF exchange and review states. The scanner can inspect public post types, Elementor data, ACF fields, menus, widgets, taxonomies and WooCommerce content. Frontend replacement is limited to normal HTML GET requests and skips sensitive contexts such as admin, REST, AJAX and selected WooCommerce flows. Yoast and Rank Math filters support per-language SEO metadata, while hreflang, canonical and sitemap foundations organise multilingual output. Optional AI providers work in small review-first batches, with credentials preferably supplied server-side. Glossary rules, context warnings and coverage checks support consistency. The solution keeps translation management central without treating generated text or automatic frontend replacement as inherently safe.

fields.description_1: SEO Shutterstock had to make stock-image selection relevant to individual WordPress pages instead of relying on disconnected manual searches. The project combines page context, search terms, Shutterstock assets, review steps and structured image placement. That workflow needs care because licensing, file downloads and media assignments affect both content and WordPress data. The project also needed to avoid presenting image choice as a guaranteed SEO improvement. The portfolio explanation therefore focuses on the operational problem: finding suitable visuals for a page, reviewing them in context and placing licensed media into the correct content fields. The workflow also needed to remain understandable for administrators managing many pages. Clear source boundaries, review before writes and accurate media handling mattered more than broad ranking or conversion claims.
fields.description_2: I structured SEO Shutterstock as a page-aware WordPress image workflow rather than a standalone stock-search screen. Administrators can start from page or keyword context, review Shutterstock suggestions and connect selected licensed assets to the relevant WordPress or ACF image location. Search, review, licensing and assignment remain separate steps so external assets are not treated as automatically suitable. Downloads and media imports need valid file information before WordPress stores them, while capability checks protect higher-risk actions. Existing usage information helps reduce repeated selections across larger content sets. The portfolio solution describes what the project supports: contextual image research and controlled placement inside WordPress. It deliberately avoids claiming that a particular image, filename or stock source produces ranking gains without measured evidence.
